analysis.title: Global Energy Weekly: Blue wave cools off red hot energy
key_insights: Affordability and the Iran and Russia wars were key voter issues in the midterms. Fuel prices are tied to global benchmarks, so voters felt higher pump prices even though the US is a net energy exporter.

Georgia, Ohio and Texas elected governors who support a moratorium or pause on data centers. Together they hold more than 40% of potential US data center projects, so state results are likely more consequential for data center buildout than federal results.
10 states representing nearly half the current data center backlog elected governors who support a moratorium or pause on data centers.
Projects are clustering just below ERCOT's 75MW large-load threshold for the Batch Zero process. BofA would not be surprised to see politicians lower the threshold.

The federal budget is funded by a continuing resolution through December 11. The US is on pace to hit the debt ceiling in spring or summer 2027. Democrats gain leverage when the new Congress convenes January 3, which sets the path of energy policy.
Democrats may push to resume renewable energy subsidies next year, but the President holds veto power. OBBBA subsidies for renewables and batteries phase out at the end of 2027.

Congress could restrict military funding or require US troop withdrawal from the Middle East, but a presidential veto is possible and existing appropriations could fund operations. BofA expects President Trump can likely continue Middle East operations, which keeps oil and refined product prices exposed.

Pre-war global inventory buffers have been shrinking, and refined products face supply threats in Russia (Ukrainian attacks on refineries) and the Middle East. The quickest path to lower fuel prices is ending the wars, but a quick peace is not assured.

US refinery utilization is at its highest in years, yet retail diesel is at record highs and gasoline is just under 2022 levels. Low domestic stocks and export pull tie US prices to international benchmarks.

Global refinery utilization has averaged ~78% this year, the lowest since 2020, against just over 80% in each of the past 4 years. Little new refinery capacity has been added. Capacity would take years to build and producers may hesitate because cracks would compress if either war ends.

Politicians have floated a diesel export ban, which Trump has not implemented. BofA equity colleagues estimate a ban would eventually cut refinery run rates and could cause a self-imposed gasoline shortage.

Consumer relief measures are marginal. The diesel dyed-fuel tax waiver saves about $0.24/gal, only ~15% of the year-over-year rise in retail diesel. Jones Act waivers run through November 15. Looser RVP butane blending may have cut gasoline prices by ~$0.1-0.2/gal, but the butane rally has reduced that benefit.
Oil rig activity has not responded to higher prices because E&Ps are wary of volatility. Any Hormuz resolution would likely pressure oil and make shale producers less willing to add activity.
The US SPR is at its lowest level since the early 1980s. Buying beyond agreed exchanges needs a budget allocation, so refilling would need Democratic support in a lower oil price scenario.

The administration used the Defense Production Act to advance the Constitution Pipeline. The proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 to speed pipeline review has not passed. US gas production is up about 50% in a decade while storage capacity is nearly unchanged and pipeline capacity grew ~1% since 2021.
BofA does not expect a Democratic Congress to stop already-permitted LNG projects under construction, citing the failed 2024 attempt to pause LNG permits.

Solar and wind supplied nearly all US capacity additions in the past decade. BofA says baseload gas or nuclear is likely needed for data center load growth. Grid investment hit a record ~$118B in 2025, up more than 50% from 2021, and is feeding rising power bills.

sector_views.rationale: Supply is tight (shrinking inventories, refinery disruptions, low global utilization), but a Hormuz or Russia-Ukraine resolution would pressure crude and compress cracks.
Approved LNG projects under construction are unlikely to be blocked, US LNG exports keep expanding, and baseload gas demand rises with data centers.
Subsidies phase out at the end of 2027 but could be reinstated by a Democratic Congress, with a veto risk.

risk_factors: Ongoing Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts disrupting crude and refined product flows.
A quick peace would pressure oil prices, compress crack spreads and lower shale activity.
A diesel export ban could cut refinery run rates and cause a gasoline shortage.
Data center moratoriums and tighter large-load thresholds could slow buildout.
Budget and debt ceiling timing, including the December 11 continuing resolution deadline, shapes energy policy.
Low domestic gasoline and diesel inventories keep US prices tied to export demand.
Court challenges and a presidential veto could block congressional energy legislation.
vol_and_positioning: Oil volatility is off its YTD peak but still elevated relative to the past year or so (Oil VIX ETF index).
geopolitical: The US invaded Iran in late February 2026 and the conflict is in its 9th month, disrupting energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Russia-Ukraine war has lasted more than 4.5 years, and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries are cutting refined product supply.
The US launched a military strike in Venezuela in early 2026.
The Democratic Congress convening January 3 could try to restrict military funding or require US troop withdrawal from the Middle East, subject to a presidential veto.
Oil appears to be moving out of the Middle East, but the pre-war inventory buffer has shrunk.

tension_points.theme: Middle East resolution and oil prices
tension_points.bull_case: A resolution allowing safer, more consistent Hormuz operations would ease fuel prices for consumers. BofA's forecasts have a 1.5mn b/d surplus by 4Q27 and Brent falling to $80 in 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: There may be no quick path to peace. Pre-war inventory buffers have shrunk, refined products face supply threats in Russia and the Middle East, and Trump can likely continue operations despite a Democratic Congress.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Congress passing legislation that restricts military funding or requires US forces to withdraw, and the President not vetoing it, would change the outlook.

tension_points.bull_case: Projects may circumvent rigorous oversight, for example by coming in just below ERCOT's 75MW large-load threshold. Federal permitting reform is being pursued in the lame duck session.
tension_points.bear_case: Governors in 10 states with nearly half the backlog support a moratorium or pause, and politicians may lower the large-load threshold.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Politicians lowering the 75MW threshold would close the loophole and slow buildout.
